title: Regional Indonesian — one language, many accents
goal: Recognise the regional colours of the Indonesian you hear in Jakarta — Betawi and Jakarta slang, Javanese politeness words, Medan and Batak directness, Makassar particles and Papuan Malay — and judge when echoing them is friendly and when it is presumptuous.
bekal: understand Jakarta and Betawi forms: *gue, lo, bokap, nyokap, kagak, udeh, nyampe*
recognise *nggih, mboten, monggo*, Medan *kau, bah, kali*, Makassar *-mi, -ji, iye* and Papuan *sa, ko, su, pace, mace*
decide when to use a regional form yourself: echo, don't lead

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Traktiran di warung soto
dialogs.intro: A Friday lunchtime in late April at a soto Betawi stall behind the office. Fajar has announced he is paying. With him are Sarah, Yoga, and Ani, the programme's finance officer, who grew up in Makassar.

notes: **Gue, bokap, nyokap.** *Gue* (I) and *lo* (you) come from Betawi, the Malay of Jakarta's original inhabitants, by way of Hokkien. *Bokap* (dad) and *nyokap* (mum) are *bahasa prokem*, 1970s Jakarta street slang made by inserting *-ok-*: *bapak → b-ok-ap*. All four are fine with friends and colleagues of your age. Fajar uses them with Sarah over lunch because she has made it clear she likes it; in a meeting, with a ministry or with anyone's grandmother, they would be out of place.

**Kagak, udeh, deket, nyampe.** Genuine Betawi colour: *kagak* (not), *udeh* (already), *deket* (near), *nyampe* (to reach, arrive). The classic Betawi marker is turning a final *-a* into *-e*: *apa → ape, kenapa → kenape*. Younger Jakartans use it mostly for comic effect; Fajar, whose family has lived in Condet for generations, uses it for real.

**Dalam rangka apa?** Literally "in the framework of what?" — B1's meeting phrase (*dalam rangka…*) used jokingly for "what's the occasion?". Note the custom behind it: on your birthday *you* treat everyone (*traktir*), the reverse of Australia. *Rezeki* is "God-given livelihood, good fortune", and it is meant to be shared.

**Makassar -mi, -ji, iye.** In Makassar and Bugis Indonesian, *-mi* marks something as done or settled (*Sudahmi*, *Pergimi dia* "he's already gone"), and *-ji* softens or limits ("only, really": *Tidak apa-apaji* "it's fine, honestly"). *Iye* is the polite "yes". Many people from South Sulawesi keep these particles for life, even in the office.

**Nggih, mboten, monggo.** Javanese *krama*, the respectful speech level, leaks into Indonesian as single words: *nggih* (yes), *mboten* (no), *monggo* (please, go ahead; spelled *mangga* in standard Javanese). A Javanese student answering a lecturer with *nggih* is showing respect, and Sarah, after two years in Yogya, can't quite stop.

**Keceplosan, biarin, nyambung.** *Keceplosan* is "to blurt out without meaning to" — ideal for habits and secrets. *Biarin* is Jakarta *-in* for *biarkan* (let it be). *Nyambung* means "connected": a conversation that *nyambung* is one where people understand each other, and *nggak nyambung* is a reply that misses the point.

grammars.title: Jakarta and Betawi at a glance
body: Everyday Jakarta Indonesian and old Betawi overlap but are not the same. Fajar slides between the middle and right-hand columns depending on who he is talking to.
after: *Aye* is the humble Betawi "I", and *ente* (from Arabic) a friendly "you"; you will hear both from older Jakartans and in Betawi comedy. *Babe* and *enyak* are true Betawi words for father and mother, while *bokap* and *nyokap* are slang anyone in Jakarta may use.
⚠️ Don't mix the systems: *gue* goes with *lo*, *aku* with *kamu*, *saya* with *Bapak/Ibu/Anda*. *Gue* with *kamu* sounds like a costume.

grammars.title: Words that tell you where someone is from
body: A single particle can place a speaker on the map. These are the ones you are most likely to hear in a Jakarta office.
after: ⚠️ *Kali* is a trap. In Medan *enak kali* means "very tasty"; in Jakarta slang *kali* after a statement means "maybe" (B1 Unit 14), so *enak kali* = "it's probably tasty". Same words, opposite confidence.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Makan malam keluarga Simanjuntak
dialogs.intro: Saturday evening. Ibu Maria, so formal at the ministry, has invited Sarah to dinner at her home in Cempaka Putih. Her husband Pak Tigor is Batak like her; their son-in-law Nando is from Jayapura in Papua.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Masuk, Sarah. Ini suamiku, Tigor. Jangan kaget, suaranya memang keras.
lines.id: Come in, Sarah. This is my husband, Tigor. Don't be alarmed, he's just loud.
lines.literal: enter, Sarah. this husband-my, Tigor. don't startled, voice-his indeed loud.

lines.speaker: Tigor:
lines.text: Horas! Jadi kau yang bikin istriku lembur tiap malam, bah?
lines.id: Horas! So you're the one who makes my wife work late every night, eh?
lines.literal: horas! so you who make wife-my overtime every night, [bah]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Horas, Pak. Maaf, justru Ibu yang bikin saya lembur.
lines.id: Horas, Pak. Sorry, but it's actually your wife who keeps me working late.
lines.literal: horas, Sir. sorry, precisely Madam who make me overtime.

lines.speaker: Tigor:
lines.text: Hahaha! Pintar kali kau menjawab. Cocoklah kalian berdua.
lines.id: Ha! You're a sharp one. You two are well matched.
lines.literal: haha! clever very you answer. suited-[lah] you-all two.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Makan dulu. Nando, tolong ambilkan piring untuk Sarah.
lines.id: Let's eat first. Nando, please get Sarah a plate.
lines.literal: eat first. Nando, please take-for plate for Sarah.

lines.speaker: Nando:
lines.text: Siap, Mama. Kaka Sarah, sa ambilkan ikan arsik, e? Ko su pernah coba?
lines.id: Right away, Mama. Sarah, shall I get you some arsik fish? Have you tried it before?
lines.literal: ready, Mum. older-sister Sarah, I take-for fish arsik, [e]? you already ever try?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Belum pernah. Tapi “sa” dan “ko” itu dari mana?
lines.id: Never. But where do “sa” and “ko” come from?
lines.literal: not-yet ever. but sa and ko that from where?

lines.speaker: Nando:
lines.text: Dari Papua, Kaka. Di sana “sa” itu saya, “ko” itu kau. Bapak-bapak dipanggil pace, ibu-ibu mace.
lines.id: From Papua. Over there “sa” is “I” and “ko” is “you”. Men get called “pace”, women “mace”.
lines.literal: from Papua, older-sister. at there sa that I, ko that you. man-man are-called pace, woman-woman mace.

lines.speaker: Tigor:
lines.text: Jadi di rumah ini ada tiga bahasa Indonesia, Sarah: Batak, Papua, dan bahasa kantor Maria.
lines.id: So in this house there are three kinds of Indonesian, Sarah: Batak, Papuan and Maria's office language.
lines.literal: so at house this exist three language Indonesia, Sarah: Batak, Papua, and language office Maria.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Bahasa kantor itulah yang membeli ikan ini.
lines.id: And it's that office language that paid for this fish.
lines.literal: language office that-[lah] which buy fish this.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ikannya enak sekali, Bu. Eh, maksud saya, enak kali!
lines.id: The fish is delicious. I mean, enak kali!
lines.literal: fish-the tasty very, Madam. eh, meaning my, tasty very!

notes: **Horas!** The all-purpose Batak Toba greeting: hello, goodbye, cheers and "long life" in one word, often said three times at ceremonies (*Horas, horas, horas!*). Saying it back to a Batak host is a small gift; you do not need to be Batak to use it.

**Kau and bah.** In Medan and Batak Indonesian, *kau* is the normal "you" between equals and not remotely rude, although Javanese listeners may flinch at it. *Bah* is an exclamation of surprise, amusement or indignation. Pak Tigor's loud directness is a regional style, not anger — which is exactly why Ibu Maria warns Sarah.

**Ibu Maria switches.** At the ministry she says *saya* and *Ibu Sarah*; at home she says *suamiku* and plain *Sarah*. Code-switching by setting is normal for every Indonesian professional, and it is a sign of trust that she lets Sarah see the home version.

**Sa, ko, su, e, Kaka.** Papuan Malay shortens freely: *sa* (saya), *ko* (kau), *su* (sudah), *tra* (tidak), *de* (dia). *Kaka* (older sibling) is the polite way to address a slightly older person of either sex, and *e* at the end is a friendly "OK?". *Pace* and *mace* are warm, informal words for men and women, a bit like "mate" and "missus".

**Siap, Mama.** *Siap* ("ready!") is the military "yes, sir" now used jokingly everywhere for "on it". Nando calls his mother-in-law *Mama*, as sons-in-law in many Christian families do. *Arsik* is Batak goldfish-carp cooked with turmeric and *andaliman*, the peppery Batak spice that numbs the lips.

**Echo, don't lead.** Sarah's *enak kali* works because she is echoing her host, in his house, as a compliment. Leading with a regional form — *kau* to Ibu Maria at the ministry, *sa* to a Papuan official you have just met — would sound like mimicry. The safe rule: use regional words only after someone has used them with you.

grammars.title: Pronouns across the archipelago
body: The biggest regional differences are in the small words. Read across a row to see one idea travel from Jakarta to Medan and Jayapura.
after: Two famous traps with *kita*. In Makassar, *kita* is a polite "you" (*Dari mana ki?* — "where are you coming from?", with *-ki* as its short form). In Manado, *kita* means "I", and "you" is *ngana*. In standard Indonesian it remains "we, including you".

sections.title: A quick map of Indonesian accents

blocks.text: Every Indonesian speaks at least one regional language or regional Malay at home, and it colours their Indonesian. You do not need to speak these varieties; you need to recognise them so that an unfamiliar word does not throw you.

head: Region
What you notice
Example
rows: *teh, mah, atuh, euy*, a lilting intonation

blocks.text: *Medhok* (from Javanese) is the name for a thick Javanese accent in Indonesian. It is affectionate or mocking depending on who says it, so it is a word to understand rather than to apply to anyone.
Indonesians are delighted when a foreigner recognises their regional speech, and uneasy when one imitates it badly. The table sums up what is safe.

head: Situation
Safe?
Why
rows: it is simply how they talk
*gue/lo* in a meeting or with elders
*kau* to a Batak colleague at work
only if they use it first
normal in Medan, rough in Java

blocks.text: The deeper rule is about who sets the register. In Indonesia the older or more senior person usually decides how formal a conversation is, and the younger one follows. When a senior colleague switches into *gue/lo* or regional banter with you, that is an invitation; when you switch first, it can look as if you are claiming a closeness that has not been offered.

blocks.title: Handy reactions when you don't understand
items: *Maaf, itu bahasa daerah mana?* — Sorry, which regional language is that?
*Artinya apa, ya?* — What does that mean?
*Wah, saya baru dengar kata itu.* — Oh, that's a new word for me.
*Kalau di Jakarta bilangnya apa?* — What would people say in Jakarta?
